section.title: Judgment against the Nations
section.sectionRationale: Within the seam of the final woes and the ransomed return, chapters 33 to 35, this chapter is the dark counterpart to chapter 35's bright hope. The LORD summons the whole earth to witness a day of vengeance focused on Edom, the paradigm of hostility to God's people, before chapter 35 answers with the ransomed of the LORD returning to Zion with singing.
section.thesis: The LORD summons every nation to witness His day of vengeance, a sweeping judgment concentrated on Edom as the representative enemy of His people, and He alone can declare with certainty that not one word of His judgment will fail, for He has ordered it by His mouth and gathers it by His Spirit.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the whole earth summoned to listen; cosmic imagery of the LORD's wrath from the heavens; the day of vengeance falling on Edom; Edom's desolation becoming a haunt for wild creatures; and the climactic assurance that the scroll of the LORD will not fail in a single detail.

verses.text: Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples. Let the earth hear, and all that fills it, the world and all that springs from it.

units.label: The sword drinks its fill in the heavens

verses.text: The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. He will {{cherem|devote}} them to destruction; He will give them over to slaughter.
Their slain will be left unburied, and the stench of their corpses will rise; the mountains will flow with their blood.
All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree.

units.label: The LORD's day of vengeance against Edom

verses.text: When My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens, then it will come down upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction.

The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood. It drips with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom.
And the wild oxen will fall with them, the young bulls with the strong ones. Their land will be drenched with blood, and their soil will be soaked with fat.
For the LORD has a day of {{naqam|vengeance}}, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.

units.label: Edom becomes a haunt for wild creatures

verses.text: Edom's streams will be turned to tar, and her soil to sulfur; her land will become a blazing pitch.
It will not be quenched, day or night. Its smoke will ascend forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate; no one will ever again pass through it.
The desert owl and screech owl will possess it, and the great owl and raven will dwell in it. The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction.
No nobles will be left to proclaim a king, and all her princes will come to nothing.
Her towers will be overgrown with thorns, her fortresses with thistles and briers. She will become a haunt for jackals, an abode for ostriches.
The desert creatures will meet with hyenas, and one wild goat will call to another. There the night creature will settle and find her place of repose.
There the owl will make her nest; she will lay and hatch her eggs and gather her brood under her shadow. Even there the birds of prey will gather, each with its mate.

units.label: Search the scroll of the LORD

verses.text: Search and read the scroll of the LORD: Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate, because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit.
He has allotted their portion; His hand has distributed it by measure. They will possess it forever; they will dwell in it from generation to generation.

cherem.gloss: To devote something entirely to destruction, placing it under an irrevocable ban given over wholly to the LORD's judgment. It is the strongest word Hebrew has for total, given-over ruin, used here of the nations under God's righteous anger, and it underlines that this judgment is not random violence but a solemn, deliberate act of divine justice.

naqam.gloss: Vengeance or righteous recompense. This is not personal vindictiveness but the LORD's own settling of accounts for the cause of Zion, repaying cruelty that human courts could never fully address. Scripture reserves final vengeance for God alone, Romans 12:19, and this chapter shows Him exercising it in real history.

basic.context: This chapter is a sweeping courtroom scene: the LORD summons every nation and the whole earth to witness His day of vengeance, concentrated here on Edom, the nation descended from Esau that repeatedly turned against Israel. The imagery escalates from a sword drenched in blood to the stars themselves dissolving, then narrows to a picture of Edom's cities becoming a permanent haunt for owls, jackals, and wild goats.
basic.hermeneutics: Edom functions here as a representative example of hostility to God's people and to God Himself, so the judgment described, while aimed historically at Edom, carries a scope that reaches toward all nations and toward the final Day of the Lord. The cosmic language of the stars dissolving is Isaiah's regular way of describing the collapse of a proud power's whole world order, language the New Testament reuses for the final judgment.
basic.originalLanguages: The nations are {{cherem}}, devoted to destruction, a term for total, irrevocable ruin given over to the LORD. This is the LORD's day of {{naqam}}, vengeance, for the cause of Zion, righteous recompense reserved for God alone rather than human retaliation. The chapter closes by insisting this is written in the LORD's own scroll, gathered by His Spirit, so that not one detail of it will fail.
basic.typology: The collapsing skies and falling stars of verse 4 anticipate the New Testament's language for the final Day of the Lord, when Christ returns to judge the nations in full and final measure. Edom's desolation, guaranteed down to the last detail in the LORD's scroll, foreshadows the certainty of the final judgment recorded in the books opened before Christ's throne.
basic.christ: The cosmic collapse pictured here, stars falling like withered leaves, is language Jesus Himself uses for His own return in glory, Matthew 24:29, and Revelation reuses it for the final judgment, Revelation 6:13-14. All judgment has been given to the Son, Acts 17:31, John 5:22, so this chapter's certain, detailed reckoning against Edom is a preview of the final and complete judgment Christ will execute at His return.
basic.god: God is not a passive observer of history but its righteous judge, summoning the nations to His courtroom and reserving vengeance for Himself rather than leaving it to human hands. His judgments are neither careless nor random; He orders each one by His own mouth and gathers it by His Spirit, so that not a single detail of what He has declared will go missing.
basic.crossReferences: Obadiah 1:1-21 pronounces a similar judgment on Edom for its violence against Jacob. Malachi 1:2-4 recalls this desolation as proof of the LORD's love for Jacob over Esau. Matthew 24:29 and Revelation 6:13-14 reuse this cosmic collapse imagery for the final Day of the Lord. Romans 12:19 reserves vengeance for God alone.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows the LORD as judge of every nation, reserving vengeance for Himself and guaranteeing His judgments down to the last detail. It previews the final Day of the Lord, when Christ, to whom all judgment has been given, will complete exactly this kind of reckoning against every power that has set itself against God and His people.

context.literary:
Isaiah 34 and 35 are a matched pair, and this chapter is the dark panel. Read together they form a hinge at the end of the first great division of the book: one land turned to burning pitch, another turned to a garden. The chapter itself falls into four movements. A summons to the whole earth, verse 1. A sweeping sentence on the nations and the heavens, verses 2 to 4. A narrowing to Edom, verses 5 to 15, which itself divides into the slaughter at Bozrah, verses 5 to 8, and the long desolation, verses 9 to 15. And a closing appeal to a written scroll, verses 16 and 17.

The movement from the universal to the particular is deliberate. Edom stands inside a courtroom in which every nation has been called as witness. The sacrificial language, 'the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah,' verse 6, turns the battlefield into an altar, and the lambs, goats and rams of verse 6 are the animals of the altar, as in Leviticus 3. Slaughter is described in the vocabulary of worship, so that Edom's fall is not random violence but an offering the LORD claims.

The second half runs on creeping reversal. Streams become tar, soil becomes sulfur, and a kingdom that had nobles proclaiming a king, verse 12, ends with only animals possessing it. The animal list in verses 11 to 15 is long and the identification of some birds is uncertain, as the BSB footnotes admit, but the point is clear: a place once for people is given to creatures, and each is allotted a mate and a place, verses 15 to 17, an eerie parody of order.
context.historical:
Edom was the nation descended from Esau, Genesis 36:1, living south and east of the Dead Sea in rugged country whose strongholds sat on cliffs. Bozrah, named in verse 6, was one of its chief cities. Israel's relations with Edom were those of kin and rivals. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness, Numbers 20:14 to 21, was subdued under David, 2 Samuel 8:13 to 14, and in the great hour of Jerusalem's fall rejoiced and joined in the looting, as Obadiah 10 to 14 and Psalm 137:7 recall.

For Isaiah's hearers in the late eighth century, Edom was one among many small states pressed by Assyria. Placing it here, after the Assyrian crisis has been described, makes it an example. The text itself says the nations are all under the ban and then lets Edom bear the weight, which shows that Edom is a representative of the proud nations that glory in the downfall of God's people.

The ban, cherem, belongs to Israel's holy war practice, in which a city was given wholly to the LORD, Joshua 6:17. The prophets often use that vocabulary of the LORD's own campaign against enemies. The desolation described here, burning pitch, smoke rising, lonely owls and jackals, borrows the memory of Sodom, Genesis 19:28, and is paralleled in oracles on Edom in Jeremiah 49:17 to 18 and Ezekiel 35. The region later took the Greek and Roman name Idumea, though Isaiah's picture is of a theological verdict and not a travel report.
context.canonical:
Chapter 34 is the counterpart of the vision of 'the day of the LORD' that the prophets keep returning to. Isaiah had already described the heavenly powers and the kings of the earth being punished in 24:21 to 23. Here the cosmic dissolution of verse 4 is a repeat of that scene, now focused on a particular enemy. Edom's fate then recurs across the Prophets: Jeremiah 49:7 to 22, Ezekiel 25:12 to 14 and chapter 35, Amos 1:11 to 12, Obadiah in full, and Malachi 1:2 to 4, where Edom's ruin is cited as evidence of the LORD's love for Jacob.

The New Testament takes the chapter's two great images and rehearses them. The rolled-up heavens of verse 4 appear in Revelation 6:13 to 14, where the stars fall 'like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind' and the sky 'receded like a scroll being rolled up,' and Jesus' Olivet teaching uses the same cluster in Matthew 24:29. The 'smoke ascending forever' of verse 10 shows up in Revelation 14:11 and 19:3. The bloodied garment and the winepress of Bozrah in Isaiah 63:1 to 6 return in Revelation 19:13 to 15.

Isaiah 61:2 holds the other half of the phrase. 'A day of vengeance of our God' stands next to 'the year of the LORD's favor.' Here the day of vengeance is 'a year of recompense for the cause of Zion,' and the two chapters, 34 and 35, are a pair of that same pairing. It is striking that when Jesus read Isaiah 61 in the synagogue he stopped before the vengeance clause, Luke 4:18 to 19, leaving the vengeance for a later day.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted his hearers to trust that history is under a verdict. Nations that gloat over God's people and crush the weak are not outside His reach, however large they look. The first reader had been frightened by Assyria and might have been tempted by envy of its success, or by the idea that the LORD had been defeated by it. Chapter 34 says there is a court above all courts, and that the ledger of what one nation did to another is kept.

The choice of Edom matters to that purpose. Edom was kin. The hurt it did to Jacob was the hurt of a brother, and it was the sort of betrayal that wounds most because it comes from the one who should have helped. The prophet shows that God notices that kind of cruelty and answers it, and that the people of God can rest from taking revenge into their own hands.

He also invites careful reading. The last two verses tell the hearer to 'search and read the scroll of the LORD,' a way of saying that what has been spoken is written down and can be checked. This is the prophet's confidence that the words are not an emotional outburst but a decree to be tested against the facts as they unfold.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what the LORD will do. It never commands Israel to destroy Edom or any other people, and the vocabulary of vengeance is attached to God alone, 'the LORD has a day of vengeance,' verse 8. That is why Paul can quote the principle as a reason for believers to refuse retaliation: 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' Romans 12:19, citing Deuteronomy 32:35.

So the chapter is not a licence for violence against a people in the name of faith. It is the ground of a different practice. Because God will put right what has been done, His people can leave justice to Him, pray for those who wrong them, Matthew 5:44, and turn to the work of mercy. The violent images are not instructions, and they are not a template for anyone else's wars. They teach that evil is not finally allowed to stand.

What also carries over is the caution against reading the images too flatly. Isaiah describes collapsing stars and a land where smoke rises forever. Few readers expect the sky to be literally rolled like a papyrus, and the chapter's language is meant to be weighed as the poetry of final judgment, even as the judgment itself is not a metaphor.

debates.question: Is the desolation of Edom to be read literally and forever, or as the language of a decisive verdict?

views.label: A literal, perpetual desolation of the land
views.case: Verses 10 and 17 say the land will lie desolate 'from generation to generation' and that none will pass through it again. Some older commentators pointed to the fact that ancient Edom's cities were abandoned as evidence that the prophecy was fulfilled in detail.

views.label: Stock language of final judgment
views.case: The smoke 'ascending forever' echoes the fate of Sodom, Genesis 19:28, and Jude 7 says Sodom suffers 'the punishment of eternal fire,' meaning a permanent verdict, not a still-burning fire in the Jordan valley. Isaiah paints a picture whose force is decisiveness, in the same way that 13:19 to 22 describes Babylon. Amos 9:12 speaks of God's people possessing the remnant of Edom, which would be odd if the land could never be entered.

debates.bearing: The picture is firm about the outcome and not meant as a land survey. The weight rests on certainty: what God decrees stays decreed. Amos 9:12 shows that Scripture elsewhere leaves a door open for Edom's remnant to be taken in by God's people.

debates.question: Does 'Edom' stand for one nation, or for the world's hostility to God's people?

views.label: A particular historical nation
views.case: Bozrah and the land of Edom are named precisely, and prophets such as Obadiah and Jeremiah pronounce judgment on Edom for specific acts, Obadiah 10 to 14.

views.label: A representative of all hostile nations
views.case: The chapter opens with the whole earth and the stars and ends with a universal ledger. The movement from 'all the nations' in verse 2 to Edom in verse 5, and from 'Edom' back to cosmic imagery, suggests that Edom is the sample case of a general principle. Later Jewish and Christian readers have often taken the passage this way.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Edom is judged for its own crimes and also stands as the type of all who gloat over God's people, so one verdict illustrates the other.

debates.bearing: Because Isaiah starts and finishes with a universal frame, the third view is the safest. The name is real, the crime is real, and the principle reaches wider than the name.

study.originalLanguages:
The word behind 'devote' in verse 2, and again 'devoted to destruction' in verse 5, is cherem, and the BSB footnote explains that its forms refer to giving over persons or things either by destroying them or as an offering. That double sense explains the sacrificial vocabulary of verse 6. In Leviticus 27:28 what is so devoted is 'most holy to the LORD.' Cherem is not secular destruction; it is a transfer of ownership to God.

The phrase in verse 6, 'the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah,' uses zevach, the normal word for a peace offering or sacrifice. The next phrase, 'a great slaughter' (tevach), is a closely related word. The same city appears in 63:1 to 3, where the blood is that of the winepress, a harvest of judgment.

In verse 8 the 'day of vengeance' pairs naqam with a 'year of recompense,' shenat shillumim. Shillumim comes from the root shalam, whose relatives include peace and payment, and is used for repaying a debt. The BSB footnote offers an alternative: 'a year of recompense for (Edom's) hostility against Zion,' since the Hebrew is compressed. In every reading, the context is a legal settling of accounts and not an outburst of temper.

Verse 11 says the LORD will stretch over Edom 'a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction.' The two Hebrew nouns are tohu and bohu, the same pair that describes the formless and empty earth in Genesis 1:2, and that return in Jeremiah 4:23 where the prophet sees the earth 'formless and void.' The sense is a deliberate undoing of creation: the builder's tools of order are used to un-make. The builder's line is the very thing used in 28:17, where justice is made the measuring line.

Verse 14 includes a creature the BSB renders as the 'night creature' with a footnote giving the Hebrew as Lilith. It is a rare word, and translators disagree about whether it names a night bird or a demon of Mesopotamian folklore. The safe point is that the verse lists creatures of desolation and the translators' uncertainty is acknowledged in the footnotes at verses 11 and 13.

The closing verse says He will gather them 'by His Spirit.' The word is ruach, the same word used in 11:2 for the Spirit of the LORD resting on the shoot of Jesse, and in 32:15 for the Spirit poured out from on high. Here the same Spirit that renews is the agent that carries out the LORD's determined word, which shows that judgment and renewal come from the same source.

typology.type: The heavens rolled up like a scroll, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah borrows the way a scroll is closed when its reading is finished. The collapse of the heavenly powers is not random chaos but the closing of an old order. John sees this scene again as the sixth seal is opened, Revelation 6:13 to 14, and Peter explains that the heavens will pass away with a roar and the elements will melt, 2 Peter 3:10. The correspondence is real, but the escalation is that Isaiah's picture belongs to a particular crisis and its pattern, while the New Testament uses it for the end of the whole age. The type falls short in that it does not name the person who will accomplish it. That person is revealed in the New Testament as the Son of Man who comes on the clouds, Matthew 24:30.

Isaiah turns a slaughter into a sacrifice, so that judgment is described in the idiom of the altar. This reverses the normal order: usually sacrifice is the way the sinner draws near, and here it is the way the LORD's justice lands on the proud. At the cross the two meet. Christ is the offering, and at the same time He takes into Himself the sentence that the sacrifice of Bozrah pictures, Galatians 3:13, so that the wrath which here falls on the enemies is borne by the Lamb. The type falls short by showing only one side, judgment on the guilty, and not yet the substitution in which the Judge Himself bears the cost.

typology.type: Edom as the enemy of the people of God, verses 5 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Edom is Esau's line, the brother who despised the birthright, Genesis 25:34, and in Isaiah 34 he stands for every power that hates God's chosen people. In Revelation the type is generalised under the name Babylon, the great harlot whose destruction is celebrated in heaven, Revelation 18:20 and 19:1 to 3. The correspondence is the same: a power that glories in violence and is brought down by the LORD for the sake of His people. The escalation is that the final enemy is not an ethnic group but an organising spirit of rebellion. The type falls short because Edom was an actual nation with actual individuals, many of whom Scripture elsewhere shows being brought in, Amos 9:12.

typology.type: The scroll of the LORD, verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The command to search a written scroll shows that God's word is accessible and checkable, a standing witness. In the Gospels Jesus Himself tells opponents to 'search the Scriptures,' John 5:39, and in Revelation the one who holds the sealed scroll is the Lamb, Revelation 5:5 to 9. The escalation is that the scroll's contents are no longer simply read but opened by the one who is worthy. The type falls short because Isaiah's readers only searched the scroll to confirm the judgment, while in Christ the scroll opens onto redemption as well as judgment.

study.christ:
Isaiah 34 is not a chapter that speaks of mercy, and the first thing to say about Christ and this text is that it will not let Him be reduced to mercy alone. The New Testament never separates His kindness from His authority. He told His disciples that the Son of Man will come in glory and sit on His throne, and all the nations will be gathered before Him, Matthew 25:31 to 32. That is a courtroom to which the nations are summoned, as in verse 1. The apostles preached that God had fixed a day to judge the world through a man He had appointed, Acts 17:31, and Jesus said that the Father had given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. So the 'day of vengeance' of this chapter has, in the New Testament, a face.

The cosmic signs matter here. Jesus quotes the language of verse 4 in His discourse on the end, saying the stars will fall and the heavens be shaken, Matthew 24:29. He does so not as a commentator on Isaiah but as the one who will do what Isaiah describes. The image of the blood-stained warrior from Edom, Isaiah 63:1 to 6, is the companion of this chapter, and John gives it to Christ: 'He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God,' Revelation 19:13. The nations are 'struck down' by the sword from His mouth, Revelation 19:15.

Yet the chapter also helps explain why the cross matters. Verse 8 gives the reason for the vengeance, 'the cause of Zion.' God does not stand aloof from the suffering of His people. The wrongs done to them are recorded. That is why Christ's own death, in which the greatest wrong was done to the one innocent person, is not the end of the account. The apostles say that God will repay, 2 Thessalonians 1:6 to 8, and that Christ will be revealed from heaven in flaming fire. The cross shows how the justice of God and the forgiveness of sinners can both be true: judgment falls, but it falls on Christ for those who trust Him, Romans 3:25 to 26.

A guard: the text names no person of the Messiah, and its images are best read in their own setting before they are carried across. The Christian link runs through the Gospel's own use of this vocabulary for Jesus, and through the plain truth that the Judge of the nations in the New Testament is the Son. The chapter is not a hidden prediction of the details of the cross.
study.god:
The God of Isaiah 34 is first of all a God to whom every nation is accountable. The opening summons, 'Come near, O nations, to listen,' assumes that He can call the peoples to a hearing and that they are bound to attend. The doctrine of creation sits underneath it. The earth and 'all that fills it' are His, Psalm 24:1, and so none of it is neutral ground. The chapter's God is not the god of one tribe among others, which is the very claim Sennacherib's envoy will make against Him in chapter 36.

Second, He is angry, and the anger is righteous and specific. Verse 2 says He is angry with the nations and furious with their armies, and verse 8 attaches it to a cause: Zion's wrongs. The wrath of God in Scripture is never a mood. It is His settled opposition to evil, and it is evoked by what is done to the weak and to His people. This chapter makes that vivid, and it should not be softened. A God who did not mind what Edom did to Jacob would not be good.

Third, He keeps His word to the last detail. Verses 16 and 17 are among the strongest statements in the book of the reliability of God's decree. 'Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate.' The reason is given in the same breath: 'He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit.' Word and Spirit, the two agents of creation in Genesis 1:2 and 3, are here the two agents of the carrying out of judgment. This is the same God who 'allotted their portion' and 'distributed it by measure' with His own hand, a precise Lord whose purposes are not vague.

The chapter holds two things in tension. God is the judge who destroys, and He is the God who, in the very next chapter, turns desert into garden. The same hand gives out the portion of the owls and the way for the redeemed. The tension is not a contradiction; it is the shape of a holy and loving God whose love for His people makes Him the enemy of those who destroy them.

For worship, the chapter calls for awe and for patience. Believers are tempted to take vengeance into their own hands, and the chapter says the matter is already in better hands, so that worship includes giving up the right to repay, Romans 12:19. It also shapes the way Christians pray for those who oppose them, trusting that a God this exact has not forgotten any wrong and will not forget any mercy shown.

crossReferences.note: A figure comes from Edom, from Bozrah, in garments stained as one who treads the winepress, and says that the day of vengeance was in His heart and the year of redemption had come. It is the same place and the same pairing of vengeance and redeeming as 34:8, now narrated from the warrior's side. It shows that the LORD acts for His people alone, without help.

Edom is condemned for violence against his brother Jacob, for standing aloof while strangers carried off Jerusalem's wealth, and for gloating over the day of disaster. It gives the specific crimes that stand behind Isaiah's general 'cause of Zion,' showing why Edom is the chosen example.

The LORD says He loved Jacob and hated Esau, laying waste Esau's hill country. Malachi cites Edom's ruin as proof of the covenant love Israel doubted. It is the later prophetic reading of Isaiah 34, treating the desolation as evidence about the LORD's character and not just as a historical event.

Edom will become an object of horror, and as Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown, so no one will live there. Jeremiah's oracle shares Isaiah's picture of a place that becomes a lasting warning, and uses the memory of Sodom in the same way as 34:9 to 10.

At the sixth seal the stars of the sky fall to earth as figs drop in a gale, and the sky recedes like a scroll being rolled up. John takes the images of Isaiah 34:4 in nearly the same terms, so that Isaiah's picture of cosmic upheaval becomes the pattern for the last day.

A great multitude in heaven cries 'Hallelujah' because God has judged the great prostitute, and the smoke from her goes up forever and ever. The language of 34:10, smoke ascending forever, is adopted for Babylon the great, showing the New Testament treating Edom's fall as a model of the fall of every power that opposes God.

Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for the wrath of God, quoting 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay.' This is the New Testament use of the principle behind Isaiah 34:8: because God keeps the account, His people are freed to bless their enemies.

On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven in the heavens and the kings of the earth on the earth. This is the earlier statement of the doctrine behind 34:4 and 34:5, where the sword drinks its fill 'in the heavens.' It shows that judgment reaches both the spiritual powers and the political ones.

The LORD rained down burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham saw smoke rising like smoke from a furnace. This is the memory behind the sulfur, pitch and smoke of Isaiah 34:9 and 34:10, so that Edom's end is described in the colours of the most famous judgment of Genesis.

The anointed one proclaims the year of the LORD's favor and the day of vengeance of our God. The pairing that Isaiah 34 and 35 spread across two chapters sits in two clauses here, and when Jesus read this in Nazareth He stopped after the first, Luke 4:18 to 19, leaving the second for His return.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 34 stands at the dark point of a story that begins with a good creation and a wrecked one. It is the answer to the question that the book of Genesis leaves hanging after Cain kills Abel and Lamech boasts of his violence: will the wrongs done on the earth ever be set right? The chapter says that they will, and that God will do it. The words tohu and bohu in verse 11 bring us back to Genesis 1:2. The creation that was formless and empty and was then ordered by God's word is, for a land under judgment, returned to formlessness. The Bible's story is not a simple line of improvement; it contains moments when the order of creation is reversed, as at the flood and at Babel, and this is another.

The chapter also continues the long conflict between the line of the promised seed and its enemies. Edom is Esau, the older twin who did not receive the blessing, Genesis 27, and who carried a grudge for a thousand years. It is the oldest sibling rivalry in the Bible, and here it is seen from the far end: the grudge does not win. The people of the promise, who looked weak and few, are the ones for whose cause the LORD acts.

Looking forward, the chapter sets the stage for the next. The two chapters are a deliberate pair. After Edom's streams turn to tar, the redeemed will walk through a wilderness where streams gush. The jackals who haunt Edom's ruins in 34:13 are the same jackals whose haunt becomes grass and reeds in 35:7. The Bible's story needs both panels, for a world with no judgment has no hope of justice and a world with only judgment has no hope at all.

In the New Testament, the Day of the Lord of Isaiah 34 is taken up and carried into the future of the whole world: the heavens and the earth that are now will be dissolved by fire, and a new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells, will follow, 2 Peter 3:10 to 13. In Revelation the fall of Babylon in chapters 18 and 19 is followed immediately by the wedding supper of the Lamb, and then the new Jerusalem. That order, the enemy undone and then the city of God, is the one Isaiah gives us in these two chapters. The sword that has drunk its fill in the heavens is sheathed so that the ransomed can go home.

quiz.q: Who is summoned as witnesses to the LORD's judgment in verse 1?

options.text: All the nations and the whole earth with everything that fills it.
options.note: Verse 1 opens with this universal summons to listen.

options.text: Only the priests of Jerusalem.
options.note: The summons is universal, not limited to Israel's priesthood.

options.text: Only the armies of Assyria.
options.note: The chapter's focus narrows to Edom, but the opening summons is to every nation, not one army.

options.text: Only the elders of Edom.
options.note: Edom becomes the specific focus later, but the opening summons is universal, to all nations and the earth.

quiz.q: Which nation becomes the specific focus of the LORD's day of vengeance in this chapter?

options.text: Edom, called the people the LORD has devoted to destruction.
options.note: Verses 5 to 8 name Edom and Bozrah specifically as the object of this judgment.

options.text: Babylon.
options.note: Babylon receives its own oracle elsewhere in Isaiah, but this chapter's focus is Edom.

options.text: Egypt.
options.note: Egypt is addressed in other Isaiah oracles, but this chapter specifically names Edom and Bozrah.

options.text: No nation is named; the judgment remains entirely abstract.
options.note: Edom and its city Bozrah are named directly in verses 5 to 6.

quiz.q: What does the description of Edom in verses 11 to 15 depict?

options.text: Its cities becoming a permanent haunt for owls, jackals, hyenas, and wild goats.
options.note: These verses describe exactly this kind of total, lasting desolation overtaken by wild creatures.

options.text: Edom's cities being peacefully resettled by its former citizens.
options.note: The opposite; the land is left desolate and uninhabited by people, given over to wild creatures.

options.text: Edom's temporary abandonment for a single generation only.
options.note: The text specifies desolation from generation to generation, not a brief or single-generation event.

options.text: Edom's transformation into a thriving agricultural region.
options.note: The opposite; the land becomes overgrown with thorns and briers, not cultivated fields.

quiz.q: What claim does verse 16 make about the LORD's scroll of judgment?

options.text: Not one detail of it will go missing, because He has ordered it by His mouth and gathers it by His Spirit.
options.note: Verse 16 makes this exact claim about the total reliability of the LORD's declared judgment.

options.text: The scroll's contents are uncertain and subject to change.
options.note: The opposite; the verse insists on the scroll's total certainty and reliability.

options.text: Only part of the judgment described will actually occur.
options.note: The verse insists that not one of these details will fail or go missing.

options.text: The scroll only concerns events already fulfilled in the past.
options.note: The scroll concerns the judgment being announced in this very chapter, not merely past events.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's cosmic imagery connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Jesus and Revelation reuse the same imagery of falling stars and collapsing skies for the final Day of the Lord.
options.note: Matthew 24:29 and Revelation 6:13-14 apply this very imagery to Christ's return and the final judgment.

options.text: The New Testament rejects this imagery as purely mythological.
options.note: The opposite; the New Testament directly reuses this imagery for a real future event.

options.text: The imagery is applied only to a past event with no future significance.
options.note: The New Testament applies it specifically to a still-future event, Christ's return and final judgment.

options.text: The imagery describes only a minor, localized weather event.
options.note: The scale of the imagery, all the stars, the skies rolled up, points to a cosmic and final scope, not a local event.

questions: The LORD reserves vengeance for Himself rather than leaving it to human hands. Where are you tempted to take justice into your own hands instead of trusting God's timing?
Edom stands here as a representative of hostility to God's people. Where might you be quietly hostile toward those who belong to God, even without realizing it?
The chapter insists that not one word of the LORD's scroll will fail. What promise of God do you most need to trust is certain right now, even though you cannot yet see its fulfillment?
This sweeping judgment anticipates the final Day of the Lord, when Christ will judge all things. How does that certainty shape the way you live today?

Edom's desolation was total and lasting, yet it was matched by Zion's promised restoration in the following chapter. Where in your own life do you need to hold judgment and hope together, trusting God for both?

translationNotes.note: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom; naming it alongside Edom itself intensifies the specificity and certainty of the judgment described.
